entities.name: Khalji dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Khalji dynasty (1290-1320 CE) was the second dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, ruling India for 30 years under three sultans. Despite its brief duration, the Khalji period was historically pivotal: Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296-1316 CE) created India's first centralized Muslim state, defeated five Mongol invasions that threatened to destroy Islamic India, introduced revolutionary price control edicts that stabilized Delhi's economy, and conquered much of peninsular India through his general Malik Kafur's campaigns.

Jalal-ud-din Khalji founded the dynasty in 1290 after the assassination of the last Mamluk sultan. His nephew Alauddin Khalji murdered him in 1296 and seized the throne — beginning a reign of ruthless efficiency. Alauddin's price controls (fixing the prices of grain, cloth, cattle, and slaves across Delhi) were implemented through a comprehensive market surveillance system using spies and inspectors, and were effective in keeping food cheap for Delhi's population — a medieval experiment in economic planning unprecedented in scale.

Alauddin Khalji's repulsion of the Mongol invasions (1299, 1303, 1305, 1306, 1308) is considered one of the great military feats of medieval history: the Mongols had conquered from China to Poland, yet Alauddin's reforms of his army (paid in cash, not land grants) created a force that repeatedly defeated them. Alauddin's death in 1316 led to the dynasty's rapid collapse under his eunuch general Malik Kafur's manipulation, ending in the Tughluq dynasty's rise in 1320.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alauddin Khalji's repulsion of five Mongol invasions saved Islamic India from the destruction wrought on Persia, Iraq, and Central Asia, while his market price controls represent medieval history's most ambitious experiment in state economic management.
